sections.title: Infantile Nystagmus Syndrome (INS)
content: Onset: Birth to 6 months.
Waveform: Typically horizontal, conjugate, and stays horizontal in up/down gaze.
Accelerating Slow Phase: Pathognomonic feature on electronystagmography (ENG).
Null Point: Position of least intensity where VA is best; often leads to compensatory head turn.
Inverted OKN: Paradoxical response where the fast phase is in the same direction as the drum rotation.
Absence of Oscillopsia: Due to neural adaptation/suppression.

content.explanation: D: Damping with convergence and Decreased during sleep; W: Waveform (accelerating slow phase); A: Abolished/Attenuated during sleep; R: Reverse (Inverted) OKN; F: Fixation effort worsens intensity.

sections.title: Latent & Manifest Latent Nystagmus (LN/MLN)
content: Definition: Nystagmus that appears only when one eye is occluded (Latent) or when both eyes are open but one is suppressed (Manifest Latent).
Direction: Fast phase beats TOWARD the fixing (uncovered) eye.
Waveform: Decelerating slow phase (unlike INS).
Associations: Strongly linked with Infantile Esotropia and the Ciancia Syndrome (large angle ET, cross-fixation, latent nystagmus).
Alexander's Law: Intensity increases when looking in the direction of the fast phase.

sections.title: Periodic Alternating Nystagmus (PAN)
content: 1. Active Phase (90s): Horizontal jerk nystagmus in one direction.
2. Neutral Phase (5-10s): Brief period of relative quiet or transition.
3. Reversal Phase (90s): Nystagmus beats in the opposite direction.
4. Etiology: Cerebellar nodulus/uvula lesions or idiopathic (congenital).
5. Treatment: Baclofen (GABA-B agonist) is often highly effective.

sections.title: Downbeat Nystagmus (DBN)
content: Localization: Cervicomedullary junction (Foramen Magnum).
Top Causes: Chiari Malformation Type 1, Cerebellar Degeneration, Lithium toxicity, Magnesium deficiency, B12 deficiency.
Clinical Tip: Worsens on down-gaze and lateral-gaze.
Management: Check MRI Brain/Posterior Fossa; consider 4-aminopyridine.

sections.title: Upbeat Nystagmus (UBN)
content: Localization: Medulla (large lesions) or Pontomesencephalic junction (anterior vermis).
Primary Position: Nystagmus beats upward in primary gaze.
Causes: Wernicke encephalopathy, MS, Brainstem stroke, Medullary tumors.
Observation: Can change to downbeat nystagmus over time in some degenerative conditions.

sections.title: Ataxic Nystagmus & INO
content: Step 1: Identify Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) via adduction deficit on the side of the MLF lesion.
Step 2: Observe the contralateral eye during abduction.
Step 3: Note 'Ataxic' horizontal jerk nystagmus in the abducting eye.

Mechanism: Interruption of the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) preventing excitatory signal to the contralateral medial rectus, with compensatory 'over-firing' to the lateral rectus (Hering's Law).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Comprehensive History: Age of onset, oscillopsia, family history, drug/toxin exposure.
2. Clinical Exam: VA (monocular vs binocular), head posture, waveform direction, presence of null point.
3. Sensorimotor: Check for strabismus (LN association), convergence effect.
4. Neuro-Imaging: MRI Brain + Orbit (Mandatory for DBN, UBN, PAN, or any new-onset acquired nystagmus).
5. Ancillary: Electroretinography (ERG) if sensory INS suspected (e.g., LCA, Albinism), VEP for optic nerve hypoplasia.

sections.title: Surgical Management Strategies
content: Anderson-Kestenbaum: Recession/Resection of EOMs to shift the null point to primary position to eliminate head turn.
Large 4-Muscle Recessions: Decreases the 'gain' of the nystagmus, improving foveation time and visual acuity even without a null point.
Artificial Divergence: Inducing convergence (using base-out prisms or surgery) to utilize the convergence damping effect.
Tenotomy and Reattachment: Proposed by Dell'Osso to disrupt the proprioceptive feedback loop.

sections.title: Neurological Red Flags
content: Acquired nystagmus in an adult (Always pathological until proven otherwise).
Associated Papilledema or focal neurological deficits.
Monocular nystagmus in a child (Rule out Glioma or Spasmus Nutans).
See-Saw Nystagmus (Chiasmal/Parasellar lesions).
Sudden onset Oscillopsia.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: In albinism, the nystagmus is usually INS-type and is sensory-defect related.
Nutational movements (head nodding) in Spasmus Nutans are often compensatory but don't always match the frequency of the eye movements.
Always measure monocular VA in INS patients using high-plus lenses to blur the other eye rather than an occluder, to avoid triggering latent nystagmus.
